title: Recycled vs Recyclable Packaging Boxes: A Buyer’s Guide
seoTitle: Recycled vs Recyclable Packaging Boxes: Buyer’s Guide
summary: Compare recycled content and recyclability in custom packaging boxes. Define claim boundaries, supplier evidence and finished-box approval requirements.
intro: Recycled packaging describes material inputs; recyclable packaging describes a possible end-of-life route. Buyers should assess them separately. Define whether each claim covers the board, wrapping paper, insert or complete box, then request evidence for that boundary. A recycled-content statement does not establish recyclability, and a recyclable design does not tell you how much recycled material it contains. Review the destination market and the finished construction before approving public wording.
cta: For projects starting at 1,000 pieces, send your box or product dimensions, quantity, destination market and proposed recycled-content wording. Include available material documents so MTT can review component options and identify evidence gaps before sampling.
sections: The two questions belong in different columns

Recycled content asks what went into a material. Recyclability asks what can happen to the used packaging in an applicable collection and recycling system. A purchasing team can pursue both objectives, but approving one does not approve the other. Nor does either establish that the complete packaging has a lower environmental impact than an alternative.

For a rigid gift box, separate the structural board from the wrapping paper, insert, closure and accessories. The board may have documented recycled content while the wrap has a different specification. A statement covering the board cannot automatically describe the complete box, much less a set that also includes a ribbon, shopping bag and product.

Start the brief with two fields: the recycled-content requirement and the intended end-of-life objective. Add the destination market.
Define what the percentage covers

Before comparing recycled-content figures, ask for the material name, component, stated percentage, calculation basis and supporting document. Record whether the supplier distinguishes pre-consumer and post-consumer material. Do not infer that distinction from the colour of a paper sample or from a description such as natural kraft.

The denominator is the most easily overlooked part. Is a percentage based on the fibre in the wrapping paper, the mass of the board, or the complete assembled packaging? These are different boundaries. Ask the supplier to write the boundary in the quotation and material schedule, including any excluded components.

An illustrative comparison shows the problem. One quotation specifies recycled content for the greyboard; another specifies it for a paper insert. Neither figure tells the buyer which complete box has more recycled material. Keep the claims separate until a comparable calculation is available.
Build a small evidence table

Use one line per component rather than one environmental description for the order. The list should include structural board, wrap, liner, insert and separate bag.

For each line, record: material reference; recycled-content statement and scope; document reference; recycling question still open; approval owner. A blank cell means unknown, not zero and not accepted.

Documents should identify the material actually proposed for the order. Keep the approved material reference with the purchase specification.
Treat recycling as a finished-construction question

A rigid box combines materials through wrapping, gluing and decoration. Review the actual construction and the intended disposal sequence. A removable tray can be assessed separately from a bonded tray, but removability alone does not prove that either component is accepted by a local system.

The 4evergreen Circularity by Design Guideline addresses conventional, flotation-deinking and specialised recycling pathways. That distinction is a useful reminder to identify the relevant process rather than assuming one universal route for paper packaging. The guideline is a design reference, not a certificate for a particular box.

Ask whoever supplies recycling evidence to identify the specimen and its limitations. Does the assessment cover the decorated box, only its paper, or a different construction? If the insert, coating or closure changes, decide whether the existing evidence still applies. Check collection acceptance for the intended market separately from material behaviour in a test.
Keep purchasing language separate from pack copy

An internal target can be provisional: request a documented recycled-content option for the structural board. A printed claim is a public statement about a defined item. Do not transfer wording from an early quotation into artwork without confirming its scope and support.

For US-facing claims, the FTC Green Guides summary calls for qualification of partial recycled-content claims and recyclable claims where appropriate facilities are not sufficiently available. It also cautions against broad, unqualified environmental benefit claims. Review the requirements of each destination before approving pack copy.

A useful approval record keeps the proposed wording beside its evidence, component boundary and target market. If the evidence only concerns the insert, name the insert. Avoid allowing a paper-related statement to appear as though it describes the bottle, cap or complete gift set.
Compare equivalent packaging, not only material descriptions

Keep the same product, packing quantity and protection requirement when comparing proposals. A change in board or paper can require another assessment of appearance, folding, wrapping and fit.

For a perfume presentation box, review bottle support and removal with the intended insert. For a jewellery box, inspect the contact surfaces and the way small items are retained. Ask for representative samples and agree acceptance criteria before choosing on the strength of an environmental description alone.

The custom insert options page provides a starting point for discussing support geometry. A lighter insert that cannot hold the product securely is not an equivalent proposal. Equally, adding material without a defined protective function deserves review. Record the reason for each structural choice.
Close the evidence gap before placing the order

The final purchasing question is whether the approved box and the approved statement refer to the same specification. Match the material schedule, sample revision, artwork and order documents. Assign an owner to any unresolved sourcing or disposal question, and set a decision point before production approval.

Use the finished-box approval checklist for the broader review of structure, protection and documentation. This comparison supplies the terminology and claim boundaries that belong inside that process.

Keep three outcomes available: accept the documented proposal, request a specific revision, or retain the material while withholding an unsupported public claim. That last option avoids forcing an evidence gap into a yes-or-no judgement about the physical packaging. The box can be evaluated on its actual performance while the environmental wording remains unapproved.

title: Packaging Boxes Without Plastic Lamination: What to Specify
seoTitle: Packaging Boxes Without Plastic Lamination: Buyer Guide
summary: Specify packaging boxes without plastic lamination. Review surface treatments, scuffing, wrapped edges, sample acceptance and environmental claim limits.
intro: To specify packaging boxes without plastic lamination, identify the surfaces covered by the requirement and request the complete alternative finish specification. Approve a decorated, assembled sample against agreed handling and appearance criteria. Removing a laminate does not automatically make the box plastic-free or recyclable: coatings, adhesives, inserts and accessories still need review. Keep the surface-performance decision separate from any environmental statement printed on the packaging.
cta: For projects starting at 1,000 pieces, send the current box specification, artwork, dimensions, quantity and expected handling conditions. MTT can review candidate paper and finish options and the sample checks needed before approving a lamination change.
sections: Write the requirement so the supplier can price it

A request for packaging boxes without plastic lamination needs a defined boundary. Does it cover the exterior wrapping paper, the inner liner and insert, or every part of a gift set? Identify the surface and the film process you intend to remove.

Ask for the full proposed finish specification, including any coating, varnish, adhesive and decorative transfer. A matte appearance does not reveal whether a film is present. Likewise, water-based describes part of a formulation or process; it does not by itself establish that the finished construction is plastic-free or recyclable.

Use a precise purchasing instruction: quote the exterior wrap without an applied plastic laminate and identify all alternative surface treatments. Keep environmental copy out of the artwork until the selected construction has been reviewed.
Choose the surface around its real handling

List how the box will be handled before selecting a finish. Will it be packed directly into a shipping carton, displayed under retail lighting, repeatedly opened, or placed inside a paper bag? Which surfaces rub against the insert, lid, sleeve or neighbouring box?

Consider the following comparison as a starting point for discussion, not a universal performance ranking. An uncoated textured wrap may suit a tactile presentation, but its appearance should be checked after the intended handling. A printed wrap with a specified coating may offer a different feel and surface response.

The buyer's task is to approve an acceptable result, not to assume that every unlaminated surface behaves alike. Paper grade, colour coverage, decoration, adhesive and conversion all belong to the sample specification.
Look first at edges and contact points

Broad flat surfaces can look convincing in a photograph while vulnerable areas remain unexamined. Inspect wrapped corners, folded edges, the lid contact line and the area around a pull ribbon or finger opening. These are useful places to check for marking, cracking, lifting or visible colour change during the agreed handling review.

For a drawer box, examine the actual sliding fit rather than only a loose paper swatch. For a lift-off lid, repeat the intended opening action and inspect the contact surfaces. If the assembly binds, review dimensions and construction; a finish change should not be used to conceal a fit problem.

Record any defect with its location and conditions. “The surface marks” is too vague to guide a revision. A photo of the contact line, matched to the sample reference and handling sequence, gives the supplier a more useful starting point.
Make a finish acceptance brief

Agree the checks before judging competing samples. Include the intended product, box revision, surface treatment, lighting for visual review and conditions of handling. Specify which observations are unacceptable and which can be compared against an approved reference.

A practical review can examine appearance before and after representative rubbing, product removal and packing. Where damp handling is relevant, agree a suitable assessment with the supplier; do not improvise a liquid exposure and present it as a recognised test.

Keep the exercise bounded. A desk review can reveal a visible scuff or assembly issue, but it cannot prove transport performance or recyclability. Ask for separate evidence when either claim is part of the purchasing decision.
Review decoration as part of the new construction

If the design includes foil, embossing, debossing or printed solid areas, request those features on the candidate paper. An undecorated white mock-up cannot establish how the final dark printed lid will look after handling. Nor should a paper swatch stand in for wrapped corners and glued joints.

Discuss where decoration is necessary and where the material itself can carry the design. This is a design decision, not an automatic environmental improvement. Compare the appearance, manufacturing feasibility and evidence for the actual alternatives without declaring one process universally sustainable.

MTT's sample approval checklist connects these finish decisions to the complete box. Retain a representative approved sample with the material and artwork references so that a later paper or coating substitution triggers a deliberate review.
Check the environmental statement separately

Removing one laminate does not settle the recycling question for the complete packaging. The remaining wrap, board, adhesive, insert and accessories still need to be considered. Ask what the proposed statement covers and what evidence supports that scope in the destination market.

The 4evergreen design guideline offers a framework for discussing paper packaging and relevant recycling pathways. Use it to ask better questions about the selected construction, not as permission to print a recycling claim.

For US-facing marketing, the FTC Green Guides summary explains that environmental claims need appropriate support and qualification. Keep a narrowly described material change distinct from a broad environmental-benefit statement. Other markets require their own review. Do not replace “without plastic lamination” with “plastic-free packaging” unless the broader statement has actually been substantiated.
Release a specification rather than a finish nickname

The order file should identify the paper, treatment, decoration, adhesive where relevant, approved sample and acceptance criteria. If appearance depends on a particular grade, do not allow an unspecified equivalent to bypass approval. State how a proposed substitution will be evaluated.

Ask for the assembled dimensions and packing arrangement as well. A change intended to improve the surface may add a sleeve, tissue or other protective component. Assess that addition openly instead of treating the presentation box in isolation. Check whether the alternative still meets the original material objective.

The MTT sustainability overview sets out project-dependent material questions. That record is more reliable than approving the word matte or natural on its own.
